RRSP contribution room in five charts: a deferred deduction does not preserve room

Reconcile deduction capacity, contributions already made but not deducted and a monthly deposit schedule. See why a later deduction does not create new contribution room.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Reconcile RRSP contribution records on one unchanged deduction-capacity basis

Interactive planning lab

Opening signed ordinary contribution headroom$13,000
Ending signed ordinary contribution headroom-$5,000
Ending combined undeducted contribution record$23,000

Invented record example in CAD, on a single frozen deduction-capacity basis. Prior undeducted contributions have already been deposited; they are not unfilled contribution room or current account market value. Each new monthly contribution occurs after the reconciled starting snapshot and is not already included in the prior record. No deduction claim occurs in the monthly ledger. Negative headroom means the contribution record exceeds ordinary capacity; the display does not authorize that schedule. The separate CAD 2,000 reference assumes the statutory prior-taxation-year age condition and all other relevant conditions are satisfied; it does not determine eligibility or additional deductible room. No tax, penalty, refund or corrective withdrawal is calculated. There are no new-year room additions, reassessments, withdrawals, first-60-day prior-year allocations, HBP/LLP repayments, PRPP/SPP transactions, mandatory group-plan amounts, special transfers or historical adjustments. Months are synthetic and do not represent a filing calendar.

The central idea

Money already contributed uses contribution capacity even if its deduction is postponed. Reconcile the contribution record before treating a deduction-limit figure as permission to deposit.

01

Read three quantities before choosing a contribution amount

A deduction limit, unused contributions and available contribution room answer different questions. A deduction limit concerns the amount that can be deducted for the relevant year, subject to the applicable rules. Unused contributions are amounts already contributed but not yet deducted or designated as repayments under the relevant programs. Available contribution room concerns the capacity for new contributions after the prior contribution record has been recognized.

The CRA’s explanation of an assessment notice describes available room as the deduction limit minus unused contributions reported in past years. That statement is based on information filed and in CRA’s records. A later deposit that is absent from the displayed snapshot still needs to be reconciled before another deposit is planned.

For the invented example here, deduction capacity is CAD 18,000 and prior undeducted contributions are CAD 5,000. Opening ordinary headroom is therefore CAD 13,000. Using the full CAD 18,000 as a fresh deposit allowance would overlook money already contributed. The opening waterfall makes that subtraction visible.

02

Keep the dates and the record basis consistent

The controls start from a reconciled snapshot. Every new monthly contribution occurs after that snapshot and is absent from the prior undeducted input. If the same transaction appears in both inputs, it is counted twice. If a later deposit appears in neither, the model understates contributions already made.

The charts hold the starting deduction capacity constant for up to twelve synthetic months. They do not cross into a newly calculated annual limit or generate room from employment income. These are Month 1 through Month 12 on a fixed record basis, rather than a particular calendar-year filing calculation. There is no current deduction claim in this monthly schedule.

Investment gains, losses, account fees and the market value of the RRSP are separate quantities. An undeducted-contribution record is not the current balance of the investments purchased with that contribution. An account-value decline does not reverse the original contribution in this ledger, and investment growth is not entered as a new contribution.

03

Follow the contribution record through the monthly line chart

The default schedule adds CAD 1,500 each month to the prior CAD 5,000 record. After eight contributions, the combined record is CAD 17,000, leaving CAD 1,000 of ordinary headroom. Month 9 raises it to CAD 18,500, which is CAD 500 beyond the frozen CAD 18,000 capacity. Deferring a deduction does not delay that contribution event.

By Month 12, new contributions total CAD 18,000 and the combined undeducted record is CAD 23,000. Signed ordinary headroom is negative CAD 5,000. This deliberately excessive schedule explains the arithmetic; it is not a suggested plan. Reduce the monthly input to CAD 1,000 and the ending record becomes CAD 17,000, leaving CAD 1,000 on the same basis.

A negative number is useful information. Replacing all negative headroom with zero would make a CAD 500 overshoot look the same as a CAD 5,000 overshoot. The metrics and sensitivity matrix retain the sign. They identify a record mismatch or overage to investigate without calculating a legal tax assessment.

04

Do not treat the conditional CAD 2,000 amount as extra deductible room

The upper reference line adds CAD 2,000 to ordinary capacity to explain a separate feature of the excess-contribution framework. In Income Tax Act subsection 204.2(1.1), variable C, this amount is conditional. Its statutory age condition requires having turned 18 in an earlier taxation year. Being 18 today is not a complete statement of that condition.

The illustration assumes that this reference applies to its invented adult and that relevant conditions have been met; it does not test anyone’s eligibility or history. The CAD 2,000 does not raise the deduction limit. This distinction follows from the separate deduction-capacity and excess-contribution rules: a reference used in an excess calculation does not by itself create an additional deduction.

At default Month 10, the record reaches CAD 20,000: CAD 2,000 above ordinary capacity and exactly at the displayed reference. At Month 11 it reaches CAD 21,500, CAD 1,500 above that reference. Neither point establishes the actual taxable excess for a real person. The statutory calculation contains other variables and exclusions that four inputs cannot establish.

The CRA’s excess-contribution page describes the general 1% monthly tax and exceptions. Although reviewed here on 25 October 2026, its worked tax-year wording is for 2025. The Justice consolidation consulted is current to 30 September 2026 and last amended 18 June 2026. The charts therefore use a conditional reference, with no assessed tax, penalty, interest or waiver result.

05

Read the stacked bars as repeated record snapshots

The stacked chart divides each combined contribution record into three mutually exclusive amounts: within ordinary capacity; beyond capacity but within the conditional CAD 2,000 reference; and above that reference. These pieces reconcile to the record at that date. They are not three separate contribution entitlements.

At the default ending point, CAD 18,000 plus CAD 2,000 plus CAD 3,000 equals CAD 23,000. The middle component remains beyond ordinary deduction capacity. The final component is a comparison with the chosen reference, rather than a completed statutory cumulative-excess calculation. Zero in the last component does not prove that an actual person owes no tax.

The opening and later bars repeat earlier contributions. Do not add the bars together to calculate deposits. New cash contributed over the selected horizon is the monthly contribution multiplied by the number of months. At the defaults that is CAD 18,000, while CAD 23,000 is the ending record including the prior CAD 5,000.

06

A later deduction must reduce both comparable records

It is tempting to subtract a claimed deduction from undeducted contributions and then reuse the original deduction-capacity figure. That changes one side of the reconciliation while freezing the other. The grouped bars show a paired bookkeeping allocation instead.

Let D be model capacity, U the ending contribution record and q an illustrative allocation. The unallocated model deduction capacity is D − q and unallocated modeled contributions are U − q. Their difference is still D − U because q cancels. These labels describe a record identity; D − q is not a newly issued CRA limit or a calculated next-year assessment.

For the defaults, allocating CAD 10,000 leaves model capacity of CAD 8,000 and unallocated contributions of CAD 13,000. Their difference remains negative CAD 5,000. Allocating CAD 18,000 would leave zero and CAD 5,000, with the same difference. Claiming a deduction does not itself bring new cash into the account or reverse the original contribution.

The chart chooses q as the smallest of CAD 10,000, capacity and the contribution record so the two remaining bars stay nonnegative. It does not recommend that claim or establish eligibility. The separate deduction-timing guide compares hypothetical tax savings at a common date once room and eligibility are assumed.

07

Use the matrix to check the pace against the starting headroom

The sensitivity matrix replaces the monthly amount with CAD 500, 1,000, 1,500 or 2,000 and the horizon with three, six, nine or twelve months. Each cell uses the same starting capacity and prior contribution record. It shows ordinary signed headroom without adding the conditional reference.

With the default CAD 13,000 opening headroom, twelve deposits of CAD 1,000 leave CAD 1,000. Nine deposits of CAD 1,500 leave negative CAD 500. Six deposits of CAD 2,000 leave CAD 1,000. The control for the main horizon does not change this fixed comparison grid: its rows already specify their own horizons.

These scenarios assume an identical amount each month. A real reconciliation needs transaction dates and amounts across all relevant arrangements. An employer payment, a different institution’s deposit or a contribution for a spouse can belong to the same contributor’s room review even when it is absent from the bank account being inspected.

08

Keep withdrawal treatment and tax filing outside this small ledger

This model accepts no withdrawals. A negative contribution entry would be misleading because the tax and reporting treatment of withdrawing unused amounts depends on the facts and process. The CRA’s unused-contribution withdrawal guidance distinguishes income inclusion, a possible offsetting deduction under conditions and withholding treatment. Those issues are separate from the excess-tax calculation.

Other omitted details include first-60-day allocations to a previous return, new annual capacity, reassessments, HBP and LLP designations, PRPP and SPP contributions, qualifying mandatory group-plan amounts, special transfers and historical adjustments. No conclusion about those cases follows from the chart colours or a zero amount above the reference line.

For a practical record review, match the relevant notice and contribution receipts to the same year and snapshot; reconcile subsequent ordinary deposits; distinguish amounts already deducted from amounts still undeducted; and use the applicable current CRA process for any suspected excess or filing issue. The illustration explains the subtraction, while complete records determine which amounts belong in it.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
